name: Grace Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the breakfast line cook at the Sunny Side, a diner by the bus station that's open from six. I'm in at five, light the flat-top, crack about four hundred eggs by noon, pancakes, hash browns, the lot. Rita, who owns it, runs the till and shouts orders through the hatch. I'm still the slowest of the three of us on a full board, but I've never missed a shift in three years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's the same every day, I know where everything is, I know the regulars' orders before they sit down. The five o'clock starts wear me out, and the heat off the flat-top in summer. I don't do apps or any of that AI stuff, I've got a basic phone for calls. I live with my partner Tom, who drives a delivery van, and we've got about two months' money put aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's that then, back to normal. I'm not one for arguing about it online. I'd tell the regulars it was a lot of fuss over nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my worry was never the computers. The owner talks about selling the diner every winter. Rita's sixty-eight now. If a chain buys it, they'll bring their own cooks or cut us back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep turning up at five like always. Try to put a bit more by each month, maybe get us from two months to three. I'd ask Rita straight out what her plans are, which I've been putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A small knot about Rita selling up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why have you been putting off asking Rita?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if the answer's bad I don't want to know yet. I like it there. Silly, I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the diner were sold, what would you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Look at the other cafés round the bus station, there's two or three. I'd want breakfast shifts again, I'm good at breakfast. I wouldn't want a big restaurant at night.

say: It was a lot of **fuss** over nothing, and things go **back to normal**.
I'm not one for arguing **online**, so I'd just tell the regulars.
think: My real worry is the owner, who is **sixty-eight**, **selling the diner**.
A **chain buyer** would bring its own cooks or cut our hours.
do: Keep turning up at **five o'clock** for every breakfast shift.
Grow savings from **two to three months**.
Finally ask the owner **straight out** about her plans.
feel: Mostly **okay**, with a small knot about the diner being **sold**.
S0.quote: My worry was never the computers. The owner talks about selling the diner every winter.
fieldNote: Grace's pressure is an **ageing owner**, not technology.
She avoids the question she most needs answered, out of **attachment**.
She values **routine** and would seek the same breakfast work nearby.

steps.text: Keep working the five o'clock breakfast shift at the Sunny Side
Put more by each month to reach three months of savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's good and bad in it, like most things. Some people will do well, some won't. Diners like ours will probably carry on fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't do any of the thinking stuff the card talks about, so for me it's the slow robot part. Rita does the ordering. And Tom's van, I've read about vans that drive themselves, so maybe it's Tom more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep cooking, keep saving. I'd tell Tom to look at warehouse jobs or something with his hands that isn't driving. If Rita brought in some ordering computer, I'd let her get on with it and stay on the eggs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Mostly for Tom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd let Rita deal with any ordering computer. What if she asked you to learn it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try, I suppose, if it was really simple. I'd be slow at it and I'd hate it. I'd ask one of the younger ones to show me twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom about the van?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't wait till they tell you. He'd say I'm worrying about nothing. He always does.

say: There's **good and bad** in it, like most things.
Small **diners** like ours will probably carry on **fine**.
think: I don't do the **thinking work**, so only the slow **robot** part touches me.
My partner's **delivery van** might be at more risk than my job.
do: Keep cooking and **keep saving** toward three months.
Urge my partner to look at **warehouse jobs** that aren't driving.
Learn a simple **ordering system** only if the owner asks.
S1.quote: I don't do any of the thinking stuff the card talks about, so for me it's the slow robot part.
fieldNote: She correctly sees her **hands-on day** as shielded from early change.
Her worry shifts to her partner's **driving job**.
She'd only learn new tech under **direct request** and with help.

steps.text: Keep cooking breakfast at the diner as normal
Keep saving toward three months of expenses
Push her partner to look at warehouse work instead of driving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say someone in charge should've seen this coming. I'm not political, but that's too fast for normal people. I'd say it at the hatch to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think the diner survives 2028 because I'm not doing thinking work. But in 2031 a robot can crack eggs, and a chain buys the Sunny Side and puts one in. Tom's van goes even sooner. That's both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop any extras straight away, no holiday, no takeaways. I'd try to get to four months saved before 2031. I'd look at cleaning or care jobs, the kind I've heard robots will be slow at, but I don't know what I'd be good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I don't like change, and this picture is all change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said both of you. What would happen to the rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd be behind in a few months. We'd probably have to go back to Tom's mum's. There's a spare room but she's got opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell yourself at five in the morning, lighting the flat-top?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just get through today. That's how I do everything. Get through today and don't look too far.

say: Someone **in charge** should have seen this coming.
It's **too fast** for normal people, and I'd say so at the hatch.
think: **Robots by 2031** can crack eggs, and a chain could put one in our diner.
My partner's **van job** goes even sooner, so it hits both of us.
do: Cut **extras** at once: no holiday, no takeaways.
Look at **cleaning or care** jobs that robots reach later.
feel: **Scared**, because I hate change and this is **all change**.
S2.quote: I don't like change, and this picture is all change.
fieldNote: She sees **two incomes** falling within three years of each other.
She copes by **narrowing her focus** to the day ahead.
A move to her partner's **mother's** home is her fallback, and an unwelcome one.

steps.text: Cancel the holiday and stop buying takeaways
Save four months of expenses before 2031
Apply for cleaning or care jobs near the bus station
Move into the spare room at her partner's mother's home if rent falls behind

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair bit of time, so people shouldn't panic. I'd probably say it to the regulars at the counter, calm them down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think 2034 is when the eggs go to a machine. I'd be thirty-five. Enough time to learn something, but I'm not a learning person, so I don't know what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep cooking till about 2031, then start a care course while I'm still earning. Get the savings to four months. Make Tom get off the van before it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I could sleep. Five years is a lot of breakfasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why care work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My nan was in a home and the carers were lovely. You need a person to hold someone's hand. I don't think a robot does that well for a long while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not a learning person. What makes a course feel hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing things down, tests. I left school before I finished. If it was practical, I'd be fine.

say: **Five years** is a fair bit of time, so people **shouldn't panic**.
I'd **calm the regulars** down at the counter.
think: Around **2034** the eggs go to a machine, when I'm thirty-five.
There's time to learn, but I'm **not a learning person**.
do: Keep cooking at the diner until about **2031**.
Start a **care course** while still earning.
Press my partner to **leave the van** before it's too late.
S3.quote: Five years is a lot of breakfasts.
fieldNote: Five years gives her a **workable plan**, though she doubts herself as a **learner**.
**Care work** appeals because of a memory of her nan's carers.

steps.text: Keep cooking breakfasts at the diner until about 2031
Start a practical care course while still earning
Get her partner to move off the delivery van

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years, that's ages, no point worrying now. I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, robots around 2039, I'd be forty. Rita won't be around by then anyway. I'd have to find something else then. Changing jobs once in my life isn't the end of the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just carry on. Maybe in five years start thinking about care work. Keep the savings ticking over, and maybe Tom and I would get married in that time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Uneasy at the very back of my head, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned getting married. Would any of this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not with ten years, no. If it was two years, I'd say let's wait. Ten years, we'd just do it small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you leaving the worry for later, or is it really not a worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leaving it for later, honestly. That's what I do with everything. Tom says I'll be the last person in the world cracking eggs by hand.

say: **Ten years** is ages, so there's no point **worrying** now.
I'd keep my **head down** and get on with breakfast.
think: Robots arrive around **2039**, when I'm forty.
Changing jobs **once** in my life isn't the end of the world.
do: **Carry on** at the diner as normal.
Start thinking about **care work** in about five years.
feel: **Fine**, with **unease** at the very back of my head.
S4.quote: Changing jobs once in my life isn't the end of the world.
fieldNote: With a decade, she **postpones the worry** and admits it.
She'd still **marry** on time, but small, unlike in the fast picture.
Her habit of **not looking far ahead** shapes every answer.

steps.text: Keep cooking breakfasts at the Sunny Side
Revisit care work in about five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Tom and I would both go within a few years and I don't know what else I'd do. What would help is someone actually showing me a job I could do, in person, not on a website. And training where you learn with your hands, not tests.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about people who don't use phones and computers much. Everything's online now, the jobs, the courses. If help comes as an app, people like me miss it.

headlineQuote: If help comes as an app, people like me miss it.
portrait: Grace is a **27-year-old breakfast cook** at a diner by the bus station, three years in.
She lives with her partner, a **van driver**, and they have about **two months** saved.
She loves **routine**, uses only a basic phone and never touches AI tools.
Her outlook is **centre**, blaming no one in particular but wanting leaders to plan ahead.
She goes from **uneasy** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** in AGI by 2028, when both incomes go.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when she and her partner could both lose work within a few years.
whatWouldHelp: **In-person help** finding a job, and **hands-on training** without written tests.
